title: Sleep HRV, Sleep Stages, Sleep Parameters, Sleep Disturbances and Cardiovascular Risk
content:
Many sleep disorders are associated with clear, and often serious, cognitive and cardiovascular risks (CVR).
A fundamental component of sleep physiology is the adaptation of the cardiovascular, respiratory, thermal, metabolic and immune systems to the sleep stages. This function is carried out by the Autonomic Nervous System (ANS).  Brain areas involved in the different sleep stages and wakefulness are integrated with areas associated with autonomic regulation, creating consequently heart-brain interactions with mutual influences. 
Heart Rate Variability (HRV) is modulated by the sympathetic and parasympathetic system. HR modulation and its specificity in the different sleep stages is well known in healthy sleepers, with clear differences related to age, gender, physical activity and health status.
ANS changes in multiple sleep disorders are known, however a systematic use of sleep HRV and its relation to sleep stages across patient Age groups and in frequent sleep disorders is lacking.
Objectives: 1) To evaluate Sleep HRV in all sleep stages and Wake in all subjects; 2) To have several age groups of sleep disturbed patients; 3) To evaluate the most frequent sleep disturbances (Insomnia, OSAS, RLS, Periodic Limb Movements of Sleep), and their HRV specificities; 4) To evaluate, in sleep stages and HRV, parameters associated with CVR taking into account age and sleep disturbances.  
Methods: In all patients’ polysomnography (PSG) with 6 or 8 EEG channels (EMBLA equipment) was performed with standard sleep staging and HRV computed automatically by averaging successive 5 minutes intervals. Standard statistics of PSG parameters and standard HRV per sleep stage were used (SPSS version 29). 
Results: The studied population includes 405 patients. Age: Mean=48.5, SD=18.71, range 1-91 years, females 50.6% 
The following Age groups were used: Children (1-9), Adolescents (10 -19), Young Adults (20-29), Adults (30-59), Sixties (60-69), Elders (70-99).
Diagnosis were: Insomnia (n=267), OSAS (Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome) (n=267), COMISA (Comorbid Insomnia and Sleep Apnea n=70) (n=267), Sleep related Movement disorders: Restless legs Syndrome and Periodic Movements of Wakfulness (RLS/MPW n=143) and Periodic Limb Movements of Sleep (PLMS n=106), and fewer cases of Hypersomnia (Narcolepsy, Hypersomnia n=15), Parasomnias (NREM parasomnias, REM Behaviour Disorder (RBD) and Nocturnal Eating Disorder n=23), Circadian (Sleep Phase delay syndrome and Shiftwork n=20). The high total is the result of disorders overlap.
Conclusions: 1) Age related changes in Sleep parameters of sleep disturbed patients agree with all known trends except for N3, which persisted low and unchanged across age groups. 2) HRV parameters changed markedly with age: in Adulthood due to VLF increase and a reduction in time domain variables; this reduction increases significantly in the Sixties, together with HF, the parasympathetic tone. From Sixties to Elders the opposite occurs, raising doubts around longevity mechanisms.3) Sleep parameters in Insomnia, OSAS, RLS/MPW, PLMS are in line with current knowledge. 4) HRV changes were strongly marked and specific in all of them; 5) Data obtained in Age groups and Sleep Disorders are in line with known mechanisms of Sleep CVR 
These findings constitute an opportunity to increase understanding of sleep ageing and disease´s pathophysiology, namely via the brain-heart-ANS-sleep circuit while providing information concerning CVR of sleep disorders.
